summary.text: Lesson 2-3 of enVision Math Grade 4: adding whole numbers with partial sums and with the standard algorithm, understanding what a carried digit really is, and estimating before computing.

why.text: This is where the algorithm stops being a ritual. Partial sums shows every trade in the open; once those trades make sense, the standard algorithm is just the fast version of something you already understand.

objectives.text: Add multi-digit numbers with the standard algorithm
Add with partial sums and connect them to the algorithm
Explain what a carried digit is worth and where it came from
Recognize the fingerprint of a dropped carry

parentNote.text: Built from the Topic 2 textbook scan, Lesson 2-3. The diagnostic to watch: answers that come out short by exactly 10, 100, or 110 mean carries are being dropped — one question trains her to spot that fingerprint. If the algorithm wobbles, have her do the same problem in partial sums; the two agreeing is the confidence builder.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz in one sitting. Narrate every carry: ten of these made one of those.

cards.def:
**Add each place separately, then combine the pieces.**
• 358 + 277: hundreds give 500, tens give 120, ones give 15.
• 500 + 120 + 15 = 635. Every piece is visible — nothing is carried in secret.

**Work right to left; whenever a column passes 9, trade 10 of that place for 1 of the next.**
• It is partial sums compressed — faster, but the trades happen in small print.
• Speed comes AFTER the trades make sense, not instead of it.

**The small 1 written above a column is a real trade: 10 ones became 1 ten.**
• In 358 + 277, the ones make 15 — write 5, and the 1 above the tens IS the other ten.
• Nothing was moved for luck. It is place value doing its job.
cards.hint: Read the carry as a sentence: "ten of these made one of those."

cards.def:
**Write an estimate before the exact work, and compare after.**
• 358 + 277: estimate 400 + 300 = 700, exact 635 — close, so trust it.
• The estimate is lesson 2-2 working as a seatbelt.

questions.hint: The ones make more than 9 — a trade is coming.
steps: Ones: 8 + 7 = 15. Write 5, trade 10 ones for 1 ten.
Tens: 5 + 7 + 1 = 13 tens. Write 3, trade 10 tens for 1 hundred.
Hundreds: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Answer: 635.

ex.main: **635.** Two trades: 15 ones became a ten, 13 tens became a hundred.
ex.tip: Each carry is a trade of ten-for-one. If you can narrate the trades, the algorithm is yours.

questions.q: Adding 446 + 293 by partial sums, which three partial sums appear?
questions.hint: Add the hundreds alone, the tens alone, the ones alone.

ex.main: **600, 130, and 9 — total 739.** Each partial sum is one place value added on its own.
ex.tip: Partial sums let you add in any order and see every piece. Use them whenever the algorithm feels like a black box.

steps: Ones: 7 + 5 = 12. Write 2, trade for 1 ten.
Tens: 0 + 8 + 1 = 9. No trade.
Hundreds: 5 + 3 = 8. Answer: 892.

ex.main: **892.** One trade in the ones; the zero in the tens just takes what it is given.
ex.tip: A zero in an addend is not a problem — it adds nothing, and the carry still lands on it normally.

questions.q: In the standard algorithm for 358 + 277, a small 1 is written above the tens column. What is that 1 really worth?
opts: One ten — the 15 ones were traded for 5 ones and 1 ten
One — it is just a reminder mark
Nothing; careful adders can skip it
questions.hint: Where did it come from? The ones column made 15.
steps: The ones column made 15 — more than one place can hold.
Ten of those ones were bundled into 1 ten.
That bundle is the small 1: a genuine ten now living in the tens column.

ex.main: **One ten.** The carry is a real quantity in transit between columns, not a decoration.
ex.tip: Every carry has a value you can name. Name it and the algorithm stops being mysterious.

questions.q: A school collects 268 cans in week one and 575 in week two. Which pair — estimate, then exact — is right?
questions.hint: Round to the nearest hundred for the estimate, then add exactly.
steps: Estimate: 268 → 300 and 575 → 600, so about 900.
Exact — ones: 8 + 5 = 13, write 3 carry 1. Tens: 6 + 7 + 1 = 14, write 4 carry 1.
Hundreds: 2 + 5 + 1 = 8. Exactly 843.
843 sits near 900 — the estimate approves.

ex.main: **About 900, exactly 843.** Estimate first, compute second, compare third.
ex.tip: That three-beat rhythm — estimate, compute, compare — is the whole discipline of this topic.

opts: She dropped both carries — the ten from 6 + 8 = 14 and the hundred from the tens column never got added
She lined the numbers up wrong
questions.hint: Run the ones column and see what should have happened to the 14.
steps: Ones: 6 + 8 = 14. Write 4 — and the 1 ten must move left. Dropping it loses 10.
Tens: 5 + 8 (+1) = 14 tens. Dropping that trade loses 100 more.
Priya's 734 is exactly 110 short: the correct sum is 844.
Both trades vanished — the digits she wrote were right, the carries were not.

ex.main: **She dropped the carries — the true sum is 844.** Losing carries always leaves an answer short by round amounts.
ex.tip: An answer short by exactly 10, 100, or 110 is the fingerprint of dropped carries. Learn to read it.

questions.q: Three classes recycle 189, 204, and 367 bottles. How many altogether?
questions.hint: Add two of them, then add the third.
steps: 393 + 367: ones 3 + 7 = 10, write 0 carry 1.
Tens: 9 + 6 + 1 = 16, write 6 carry 1. Hundreds: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7.
Altogether: 760.

ex.main: **760.** Three addends is just two additions in a row.
ex.tip: You may also pair the friendliest two first — 393 + 367 or 189 + 367 — the total cannot change.

questions.q: Partial sums and the standard algorithm give the same answer for every addition. Why?
opts: Both add the same place values — they only record the work in a different order
They only match when no regrouping happens
The algorithm rounds and partial sums do not
It is a coincidence that has held so far
questions.hint: What is each method actually adding?
steps: Partial sums adds hundreds, tens, and ones separately, out in the open.
The algorithm adds the same hundreds, tens, and ones — the carries just move the pieces mid-stream.
Same pieces, same total; only the bookkeeping differs.

ex.main: **Same place values, different bookkeeping.** A method is just a way of organizing work the numbers already agree on.
ex.tip: When two methods disagree, one of them made a bookkeeping error — the numbers themselves never disagree.

questions.q: In 4▢7 + 258 = 715, what digit is hiding under ▢?
questions.hint: Work the ones column first and track what it sends left.
steps: Ones: 7 + 8 = 15 — write 5, carry 1 ten. The 715 checks out so far.
Tens: ▢ + 5 + 1 must end in 1. So ▢ + 6 = 11, meaning ▢ = 5, carrying 1 hundred.
Hundreds: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 — matches 715.
So the hidden digit is 5: 457 + 258 = 715.

ex.main: **5.** Solving backwards means running the algorithm forwards and asking what each column needed.
ex.tip: Missing-digit puzzles are the algorithm in reverse — they test whether you know WHY each column says what it says.

questions.q: Two addends each grow by exactly 100. What happens to their sum?
opts: It grows by 200 — each extra 100 lands in the total
questions.hint: Try it on a small example and watch the total.
steps: The sum climbed by 200 — one hundred from each addend.
Everything added to an addend flows straight into the sum.

ex.main: **Grows by 200.** A sum collects every change made to its addends.
ex.tip: Compare with subtraction, where growing BOTH numbers changes nothing. The two operations treat change very differently.
